angle: Volume for volume's sake worked in 2022. Here's what works now.
post_first_line: 8 minutes. That's Zach Herman's entire outreach flow.
linkedin_post:
8 minutes. That's Zach Herman's entire outreach flow.

The real story is what happened to the time that came back.

Zach put it toward more volume, mid-funnel deals, and enablement with reps on the team. Outreach quality stayed very high the whole time.

Here's the part that matters: volume for the sake of volume worked great in 2022. Zach was loading up Outreach and sending 1,000 emails a day out of a primary mailbox, and it worked.

That doesn't work today.

What works now is quality volume, done at scale. Personalization at scale comes up constantly, and Zach sees this kind of flow as how to actually accomplish it.

The shift isn't send less or send more. It's removing the tradeoff between the two.

What changed most in your outbound since 2022?

Slide 3: It worked then. It doesn't work today.
Slide 4: Now you need quality volume, and you need it at scale.

Slide 6: That time goes to mid-funnel deals and rep enablement.
Slide 7: Personalization at scale is the answer everyone keeps asking about.
Slide 8: Stop choosing between volume and quality. Get both.

lesson.title: Quality volume beats raw volume
takeaways: Sending 1,000 emails a day from one mailbox worked in 2022 but doesn't work today.
The goal now is quality volume at scale, not volume alone.
Time saved on outreach can go to mid-funnel deals and rep enablement.
lesson.exercise: Time your current outreach flow from start to finish. Then list what you'd do with the hours back, and pick one item (mid-funnel deals or rep enablement) to start on this week.

caption: Volume alone stopped working

angle: I tried stitching ChatGPT and Claude into my outbound. It was worse than doing it by hand.
post_first_line: Zach Herman spent 10 to 12 hours daily on outbound.
linkedin_post:
Zach Herman spent 10 to 12 hours daily on outbound.

The tools Zach tried to fix that made the work worse, not better.

In the past, Zach stitched ChatGPT and Claude together to make outbound as easy as possible. The output was not even remotely as good as what came from doing it by hand.

So the manual work stayed. Writing stronger emails. Making more targeted calls. Long days, just to keep quality up.

What changed is that work now takes a couple of minutes. Zach keeps coming back to one point: the quality stays strong, and it picks up on almost all of the context.

That's the bar. Faster only counts if the output is as good as what you'd do manually.

Most people accept the tradeoff between speed and quality. Zach's experience says you shouldn't have to.

Have you ever abandoned an AI workflow because quality dropped?

Slide 2: The output wasn't remotely as good as manual work
Slide 3: So the 10 to 12 hour days continued
Slide 4: Stronger emails and targeted calls took real time
Slide 5: Now the same work takes a couple of minutes
Slide 6: The quality stays strong, and context carries through
Slide 7: Speed without quality is just faster mediocrity

lesson.title: Speed Only Counts If Quality Holds
takeaways: Stitching together general-purpose AI tools can produce worse outbound than doing it by hand.
Context is what separates strong outreach from generic output.
The goal is saving hours without lowering the quality bar.
lesson.exercise: Pick one outbound task you do manually. Run it through your AI workflow and compare the result side by side with your manual version. If the AI version is weaker, note what context it missed.

caption: Faster, but not better

angle: The 17-title Boolean search SDRs still run, and what replaced it
linkedin_post:
17 titles in one Boolean search.

Zach Herman used to start every account list with that, and hope it worked.

Zach had 25 accounts to work through, one at a time, in LinkedIn Sales Navigator. Each one meant a crazy Boolean string and a quiet bet that it pulled every relevant contact.

If the search didn't turn up enough people, Zach ran it again. Then came pushing the results back to ZoomInfo and walking through the same process all over.

The new version looks different. Zach took the top 10 accounts from the list to keep it simple, then looked at the suggested contacts.

From there, the accounts can be ranked on whatever matters to you. Maybe it's funding amount. Maybe it's how many jobs they're hiring for.

The rule could be as specific as: hiring for more than 200 jobs and raised a Series C in the last 3 months. The list ranks itself on that.

The old process was not hard work. It was repetitive work that sat between SDRs and actual conversations.

What's the most tedious step in your prospecting?
carousel: Slide 1: One Boolean search. 17 titles. Fingers crossed.
Slide 2: Zach Herman ran that search on 25 accounts, one by one.
Slide 3: Not enough contacts? Run it again, then push to ZoomInfo.
Slide 4: Now the top 10 accounts come up with suggested contacts.
Slide 5: Rank them on funding amount or number of open jobs.
Slide 6: Try this rule: 200+ jobs and a Series C in 3 months.
Slide 7: The list ranks itself against your own criteria.
Slide 8: The old process was repetitive, and it stood between SDRs and conversations.

lesson.title: From Boolean guesswork to ranked accounts
takeaways: Long Boolean title searches run account by account, and you can't be sure they caught everyone.
Re-running searches and pushing results back into another tool adds repeated steps to every list.
Ranking accounts on your own criteria, like funding or hiring volume, turns a big list into a short one.
lesson.exercise: Write down your three strongest buying signals, such as funding stage or open roles, and turn them into one ranking rule. Apply it to your next 10 accounts.

caption: Goodbye 17-title Boolean search

angle: I tried ChatGPT as an SDR and it made my outreach slower, not faster
post_first_line: Zach Herman's ChatGPT experiment slowed outreach down.
linkedin_post:
Zach Herman's ChatGPT experiment slowed outreach down.

The reason had nothing to do with the AI being bad at writing.

This was around 2022 or 2023, when the first version of ChatGPT came out. The stack was already crowded: outreach tools, Zoom info, Sales Nav, Six Sense, Demandbase across the board. Then AI got thrown into the mix and everybody tried to use it.

Zach's plan was simple: get it to write better basic copy.

But it didn't remember who Zach was or how Zach talks. So the time went into coaching the tool to sound right, and the edits kept piling up.

Eventually it took more time to get the AI to write the way Zach wanted than to just write it. So Zach went back to doing it manually.

The takeaway: a general tool wasn't purpose-built for sellers. If it can't carry your voice, it adds a step instead of removing one.

And according to Zach, that hasn't changed much.

Where has AI cost you more time than it saved?

Slide 2: The stack was already crowded: Sales Nav, Six Sense, Demandbase.
Slide 3: Then AI got thrown in, and everybody tried to use it.
Slide 4: The goal was simple: write better basic copy, faster.
Slide 5: But it didn't remember Zach or how Zach talks.
Slide 6: Getting the copy right took more time than writing it.
Slide 7: So Zach went back to doing it manually.
Slide 8: A tool that isn't built for sellers adds steps.

lesson.title: When AI Slows Your Outreach Down
takeaways: A general-purpose AI tool wasn't built for sellers, and it shows in the workflow.
If the tool can't remember your voice, you spend your time correcting it.
If prompting and editing takes longer than writing, the tool is costing you speed.
lesson.exercise: Time yourself writing one outreach email manually, then time it again using your AI tool, including every edit. If the AI version takes longer, write down what the tool is missing about you or your buyer.

caption: AI made outreach slower

angle: The 6-tool prospecting workflow most AEs are a little embarrassed to admit they used to run
post_first_line: Six tools to send one email.
linkedin_post:
Six tools to send one email.

Speaker D admits the old prospecting workflow is a little embarrassing to look back on.

It started in Salesforce, with a report of accounts to reach out to. Then it was on to LinkedIn Sales Navigator to find prospects at each account and build a list.

From there, ZoomInfo imported that list into Salesforce. Then back to Salesforce, then into Outreach, where a sequence got built and the emails went out.

Because the process was so long, there was little time left to personalize. Speaker D describes the result as a spray and pray strategy.

Speaker D also points out that this is probably what a lot of people were doing. It wasn't a one-off.

The lesson: when a workflow has this many handoffs, the effort goes into moving data around instead of writing something worth reading.

Speaker D says the team is in a much better spot now.

How many tools does your outbound touch today?
carousel: Slide 1: Six tools to send a single prospecting email.
Slide 2: Step one: build a Salesforce report of target accounts.
Slide 3: Step two: find prospects in LinkedIn Sales Navigator.
Slide 4: Step three: import the list through ZoomInfo into Salesforce.
Slide 5: Step four: add contacts to Outreach and build a sequence.
Slide 6: The process was so long that personalization got skipped.
Slide 7: The result was spray and pray, and plenty of people did it.
Slide 8: Count your handoffs. That's where personalization disappears.

lesson.title: Long workflows kill personalization
takeaways: Every handoff between tools costs time that could go into personalizing outreach.
A long process pushes reps toward spray and pray, even when they know better.
Many teams ran this same workflow, so it's worth auditing your own.
lesson.exercise: Write down every tool and manual step between picking a target account and sending the email. Circle the steps that only move data, then ask which ones could go.

caption: Six tools. One email.

angle: Strategic account research used to take weeks. I built a full plan and sequence in 3 minutes.
post_first_line: 3 minutes. A full outbound plan, done.
linkedin_post:
3 minutes. A full outbound plan, done.

Zach Herman used to spend weeks on a single strategic account.

As an SDR working strategic accounts, Zach read 10K reports. Just to send one email meant hours of research. Figuring out who to reach out to at a company like Nike and how to tee it up could take weeks.

Then Zach built a full outbound plan and a sequence for Airbnb, a massive company, in about 3 minutes. The contacts looked good, so they went straight into the sequence after one more once-over.

Teams have told us they go from list to sequence around 90% faster. The end-to-end outbound workflow is what makes that possible.

The research was never the job. Getting the right message to the right person was.

What's the slowest part of your outbound today?

Slide 2: Zach Herman worked strategic accounts as an SDR.
Slide 3: Reading 10K reports just to send one email.
Slide 4: Hours of research before a single message went out.
Slide 5: Then Zach built a full plan and sequence in about 3 minutes.
Slide 6: Teams report going from list to sequence around 90% faster.

lesson.title: Collapse the gap between research and outreach
takeaways: Manual account research can eat hours per email and weeks per strategic account.
The speed gain comes from connecting list, plan, and sequence in one workflow.
A quick human review before sending keeps quality while cutting the time.
lesson.exercise: Time how long it takes you to go from a target account to a sequence-ready contact list for one strategic account. Write down each step, then mark which ones could be handled in a single workflow.
